## Verbatim syntax examples

```text
$ npm install mercury-examples
```

```javascript
const Examples = require('mercury-examples').Examples;
const Tutorials = require('mercury-examples').Tutorials;
```

```text
$ git clone http://github.com/tmhglnd/mercury-examples
$ cd mercury-examples
$ npm install
```

## Named features and syntax

The page does not provide explicit Mercury syntax examples or named features for:

- Writing notes
- Chords or harmony
- Continuous expression
- Pitch bend
- Vibrato
- Pressure
- Timbre
- MIDI CC
- Micro-timing
- Articulation
- MIDI output
- MPE output

## Stated description and design goals

- “Mercury is a minimal and human-readable language for the live coding of algorithmic electronic music.”
- The package contains “examples and tutorials for the Mercury live coding language.”
- The examples and tutorials can be “included via npm to easily access the files from a json file.”
- “This Package does not generate any sound or visuals.”
- “This is used in the Mercury environment and the Mercury-Playground, the browser based version of the environment.”
- “Contributions to the Mercury examples and tutorials are much appreciated in whatever form they come!”

## Other explicitly stated details

- Package name: `mercury-examples`
- Repository: `tmhglnd/mercury-examples`
- License: “The GNU GPL-v.3”
- License classification: “GPL-3.0 license”
- Languages: JavaScript 100.0%
- Stars: 2
- Watchers: 1
- Forks: 0
- Releases: No releases published
- Packages: 0
- No packages published

## Notes and pitch syntax

> “Mercury uses the standard MIDI notation, but with a slight twist. The notes are described in a 2-dimensional system, where the x-axis is the interval in semi-tones (0 to 11), and the y-axis is the octave offset (-3 to 7).”

> “In order to describe a pitch, the `note()` function is used and given two arguments, the interval between 0 and 11, and the octave.”

> “The origin of the coordinate system, `note(0 0)` corresponds to MIDI value 36 (when `sync_to_scale` is not applied) and this is also the default note value.”

> “`note(0 2)` corresponds with MIDI value 60 (C4, middle C, 261.626 Hz).”

> “If no octave value is provided, the default 0 is used.”

```text
new synth saw name(bass)
set bass note(4 0) time(1/8)
```

> “In this example the synth is playing the fourth semi-tone in the octave starting at 36. This results in the note 40, or E2.”

```text
ring aMelody (0 -1 -5 0 7 12 13 12)
new synth saw name(lead)
set lead note(aMelody 1) time(1/8)
```

> “The ring `aMelody` has interval values both lower and higher than the standard 0 to 11 range. Besides that, the octave is set at 1. The result of this melody in standard MIDI notation will therefore be: 48, 47, 43, 48, 55, 60, 61, 60.”

> “If an interval value lower than 0 or higher than 12 is used, the interval wraps between 0 and 11 and will respectively decrement or increment the octave.”

> “The main reason to use this system of notation for notes is to be able to re-use lists of values. These values can then be used as the basis for other list processing techniques and form new melodies for other instruments. These instruments can then also easily offset the notes to different octaves.”

## Note rings and melodic sequencing

```text
set_tempo 120
ring someNotes (3 7 12)
new synth saw note(someNotes) time(1/16)
```

> “The synthesizer is triggering its sound every 16th note, simultaneously incrementing the counter by one.”

> “After eighth notes, the played notes are 3 7 12 3 7 12 3 etc.”

```text
set_tempo 100
ring aRhythm (1 0 1)
ring someNotes (3 7 12)
new synth sine name(wave)
set wave note(someNotes) beat(aRhythm) time(1/16)
```

> “When the instrument gets triggered the second counter is incremented and looks up the next note value from the `someNotes` ring. The final result over 8 beats will be: 3 - 7 12 - 3 7 - 12. A dash means the instrument is not triggered.”

```text
ring someNotes (0 3 7)
new synth saw note(someNotes) time(1/4) beat(1 1)
```

> “The rhythmic and melodic patterns can also be truncated at a certain length. This is done by adding a second argument to the `beat()` function, specifying the reset time (using the same timing-notation as the `time()` function). In the following example the instrument plays a pattern of four notes, the counter resets every bar and the time is set to quarter notes. This will result in the pattern: 0 3 7 0 0 3 7 0, after two bars.”

## Scale mapping and harmony

```text
sync_to_scale minor D
ring someNotes (0 4 7 9)
new synth saw name(lead)
set lead notes(someNotes)
```

> “The function must have one argument, namely the name of the scale, but can have a second argument for the tonic (by default c).”

> “The function will map the used midi-pitch of all instruments to the closest pitch from the selected scale according to a lookup-table of predefined scales.”

> “In the code above the scale is set to d-minor.”

> “The internal lookup table for minor gives the following 12 values (0 0 2 3 3 5 5 7 7 8 8 10) that belong to the minor scale.”

> “The chromatic note values are then used to look for a corresponding value in this table to map to that scale, which will result in the new note list (0 3 7 8).”

> “The reader will see that the notes that do not belong in the minor scale (4, a major third, and 9, the major sixth), will be mapped to the scale values 3 and 8.”

> “The last step is offsetting the list to match the tonic of the scale, D. This means all values in the list will get 2 added to them, resulting in (2 5 9 10).”

```text
sync_to_scale major C
ring bassLine (0 7 12)
new synth saw name(bass)
set bass note(bassLine 0) time(1/16)
ring leadLine clone(bassLine 0 12 7 4)
new synth square name(lead)
set lead note(leadLine 1) time(1/16)
```

> “In the example above, three notes of the `bassLine` are re-used for the clone function and stored in the `leadLine` ring. The lead instrument then uses those values as notes in the octave 1. At the end all the notes are synced to the C-major scale.”

The paper explicitly mentions harmony-related functionality only in the following future-work statement:

> “Besides that two extra instruments, namely a looper and a poly_synth, will be added to the environment to be able to loop sounds and play chord progressions with one instrument.”

> “In the third place, when polyphony is made possible, the ring will get a multidimensional variation that can be use for chord progressions or fuzzy logic lookup tables for variations in melodies.”

No completed chord syntax or dedicated harmony/chord function is provided in the page content.

## Timing, rhythmic expression, and micro-timing

> “Writing for-loops or while conditions to create a repeating melody or beat is not necessary in Mercury. The environment is continuously running a loop, and all instruments are synced to that loop using the `time()` function.”

> “All timing is therefore relative to the global variable `set_tempo`.”

```text
set_tempo 120
```

> “The 120 in `set_tempo` is in beats per minute, measured in quarter notes.”

```text
time(1)
```

> “When a time of 1 is set (`time(1)`), the instrument gets triggered every bar, which is 4 times the time interval of the beats per minute (every 500 milliseconds). This results in one trigger every second (4*500 = 1000 ms).”

```text
time(4)
```

> “A time of 4 (`time(4)`) means trigger this instrument every 4 bars (4*(4*500) = 4000 ms).”

```text
time(1/4)
```

> “A smaller timing can be made as a floating-point value or a fraction. For example `time(1/4)` will result in a quarter-note beat, which corresponds to the beats per minute of 120 (every 500 ms).”

```text
time(5/13)
```

> “Complex timings can be made with all other rational numbers. For example a time of 5/13 (`time(5/13)`) will result in a timing interval of 769.23 ms, ((60000/120*4) * (5/13)).”

```text
set_tempo 120
new sample kick_909 time(1/4) //this kick is played every quarter note
new synth sine time(4) //this sine synth is triggered every bar
new sample hat_909 time(5/13) //this hihat is triggered every 769.23 ms
```

The paper gives polyrhythm examples:

```text
set_tempo 100
ring rhythmPattern (1 0.9 0.2)
new sample snare_909 time(3/16) beat(rhythmPattern)
new sample hat_909 time(1/8)
```

> “The example above shows a polyrhythmic pattern of 3 16th notes against 1 8th note.”

> “When combined with the `beat()` function, every trigger of the timing will look up the next value from a ring provided to `beat`. This allows for combination of pre-written patterns, combined with fuzzy logic, combined with complex timing.”

The paper describes timing ratios but does not identify them as micro-timing, swing, groove, or per-event timing offsets.

## Beat, probability, and articulation-like triggering

```text
ring aRhythm (1 0 1)
new sample hat_909 beat(aRhythm) time(1/16)
```

> “The 1 will represent a TRUE value, and result in the triggering of the instrument, a 0 represents a FALSE value and will be ignored.”

> “After 8 beats, this results in the following pattern: x - x x - x x -.”

```text
set_tempo 90
ring fuzzy (1 0 0.3 0.2)
new sample kick_909 beat(fuzzy) time(1/16)
```

> “These probability lists, also referred to as templates, are constructed with floating-point values from 0 to 1. Here a one means, always play this note, a zero means don’t play the note, and all values in between are a probability the note will or will not get played.”

> “The kick sample will always be played on the first count (every quarter note), will never be played on the second count (2nd 16th note), and on the third and fourth 16th note will play respectively 30 and 20 percent of the time.”

The paper does not describe velocity articulation, accent syntax, legato, staccato, note length, aftertouch, or per-note articulation controls.

## Sound and timbre parameters

> “Besides the already described functions such as `note()/pitch()`, `time()/timing()` and `beat()/rhythm()`, the other functions are `amp()/gain()` for amplitude, `envelope()/shape()` for setting the envelope, `filter()/cutoff()` for applying a lowpass filter and `add_fx()` for adding sound effects such as overdrive, reverb or delay.”

Available named parameter aliases and functions:

- `note()` / `pitch()`
- `time()` / `timing()`
- `beat()` / `rhythm()`
- `amp()` / `gain()`
- `envelope()` / `shape()`
- `filter()` / `cutoff()`
- `add_fx()`

```text
set_tempo 80
new synth saw name(rumble)
set rumble note(-4 0) envelope(10 10000) time(2)
set rumble filter(2 1500 300 0.5)
set rumble add_fx(drive 4) add_fx(reverb 2 9)
```

> “When choosing a synth, the user has to choose a waveform as a starting point. This can be a sine, triangle, saw or square.”

> “All these have various parameters that can be modified by calling their function.”

The paper does not provide syntax for continuous timbral modulation, oscillator vibrato, pressure, MIDI CC, pitch bend, or per-note timbre.

## Random and generative note material

```text
set_random_seed 8429
ring randomNotes random(8 12)
```

> “The list function `random()` will return a ring of 8 values, with random numbers between 0 and 12 (excluding 12).”

> “This will always result in the ring (11 3 6 6 2 0 0 10), when using 8429 as a seeding value, and the random function has not been called earlier in the code.”

```text
set_random_seed 8429
ring moreNotes random(3 12)
ring randomNotes random(8 12)
```

> “The `moreNotes` ring will have the first three values (11 3 6), and the `randomNotes` will be filled with (6 2 0 0 10 9 10 3).”

- Ring arrays
- Fuzzy logic

## MIDI and MPE output

Explicit MIDI-related details:

- Mercury uses “standard MIDI notation” with its own two-dimensional interval/octave representation.
- `note(0 0)` corresponds to MIDI value 36 when `sync_to_scale` is not applied.
- `note(0 2)` corresponds to MIDI value 60, C4/middle C, 261.626 Hz.
- The paper refers to “midi-pitch” mapping in `sync_to_scale`.
- The global function `sync_to_scale` can sync “all midi notes to a certain scale and tonic.”

```text
sync_to_scale minor_harmonic A#
```

No MIDI output protocol, MIDI device routing, MIDI channel assignment, MIDI message syntax, MIDI note-on/note-off syntax, MIDI CC output, or MPE output is described. MPE is not mentioned in the page content.

## Continuous expression

The page content does not provide named features or syntax for:

- Pitch bend
- Vibrato
- Pressure
- Aftertouch
- Timbre control
- MIDI CC
- MPE dimensions
- Continuous controllers
- Per-note expression
- Continuous parameter curves
- Modulation of parameters by another instrument’s audio signal

A related future-work item is explicitly stated:

> “A feature that allows for modulation of parameters with the audio-signal of other instruments instead of looked-up values from a ring is also on the todo list.”

The paper does not state that this feature has been implemented.

## Stated design goals

- “quick and hands-on composing, performing and communicating of live-coded music and sound”
- Provide “a highly abstracted programming language for music and sound complemented by visuals.”
- Allow a higher level of abstraction so “the coder does not need to write large amounts of code.”
- Improve audience comprehension.
- Keep transparency toward the audience.
- Support quick generation of the first sound during a live performance.
- Allow the performer to move quickly to compositional aspects.
- Combine given functions as desired.
- Provide “an ‘immediate code and run aesthetic’.”
- Make the environment functional as a sequencer so the performer can immediately make sound after coding the first instrument.
- Guarantee sound output through initial parameter values for instruments.
- Support algorithmic composition through generative and transformational list functions.
- Use musical words for parameters, settings, and functions to improve transparency.
- Complement projected code with visual objects related to audio and instruments.
- Preserve speed of typing code with shortcut keys.
- Reuse lists of values across instruments and octaves.
- Improve musicality by exposing instruments to global tempo, scale, and random-seed parameters.

## Stated limitations and restrictions

- The entire code needs to be run to hear changes take effect.
- This is done with the shortcut key `CMD + R`.
- Variables must be declared before instantiation of a new instrument if that instrument needs to use the variable.
- All rings are global variables.
- The environment does not allow more than 30 lines of code.
- Text automatically resizes when more lines or characters are added so that all text remains visible.
- The performer is forced to delete lines when working on a new part of the composition.
- Mercury was still “in its prototyping phase” and “is a ongoing project.”
- More synthesizers, sound-design libraries, visual libraries, and algorithmic-composition technique libraries were planned.
- A looper and a `poly_synth` were planned but not yet described as available.
- Polyphony was described as future work.
- The paper does not describe implemented chord-progressions syntax.
- The paper does not describe implemented MPE or continuous-expression output.

## Unpitched notes

- `<unpitched>` represents percussion and other unpitched instruments.
- `<display-step>` and `<display-octave>` indicate where the note should appear on the staff, based on the current clef.
- The `<pitch>` element is not used for notes with no definite pitch.
- Percussion clef is treated like treble clef when determining `<display-step>` and `<display-octave>`.

```xml
        <unpitched>
          <display-step>B</display-step>
          <display-octave>3</display-octave>
        </unpitched>
```

With percussion clef instead of bass clef:

```xml
        <unpitched>
          <display-step>G</display-step>
          <display-octave>5</display-octave>
        </unpitched>
```

A cowbell note on a one-line staff:

```xml
        <unpitched>
          <display-step>E</display-step>
          <display-octave>4</display-octave>
        </unpitched>
```

The first kick drum note:

```xml
      <note default-x="78">
        <unpitched>
          <display-step>A</display-step>
          <display-octave>2</display-octave>
        </unpitched>
        <duration>2</duration>
        <instrument id="P1-X2"/>
        <voice>2</voice>
        <type>quarter</type>
        <stem default-y="-65.5">down</stem>
      </note>
```

## Staff lines

- Staves may be more or less than 5 lines high.
- A one-line staff is specified using `<staff-details>` and `<staff-lines>`.
- For a one-line staff, the G in octave 4, treated according to the percussion clef’s treble-clef behavior, is one imaginary line above the staff.

```xml
      <attributes>
        <divisions>2</divisions>
        <key>
          <fifths>0</fifths>
          <mode>major</mode>
        </key>
        <time symbol="common">
          <beats>4</beats>
          <beat-type>4</beat-type>
        </time>
        <clef>
          <sign>percussion</sign>
        </clef>
        <staff-details>
          <staff-lines>1</staff-lines>
        </staff-details>
      </attributes>
```

## Multiple instruments per part

- Multiple instruments sharing one part are represented with more than one `<score-instrument>` element within a `<score-part>`.
- Each note can contain an `<instrument>` element referring to a `<score-instrument>`.
- The `<score-instrument>` `id` must be unique throughout the entire piece.
- Two `<score-part>` elements cannot each have a `<score-instrument>` element with the same `id`.
- Instrument names may be generated in forms such as `"P1-X2"` to make unique names easy to generate.
- More readable names may also be used if they remain unique across the entire piece.

## MIDI playback

- A `<midi-instrument>` element is added for each `<score-instrument>`.
- A `<midi-channel>` of `10` is used for each instrument in the General MIDI example.
- `<midi-unpitched>` indicates the MIDI pitch corresponding to a particular sound in a General MIDI drum kit.
- Notes include an `<instrument>` element to indicate which instrument is used and how to play it back using MIDI.
- The page does not mention MIDI/MPE output or MPE-specific features.

```xml
  <part-list>
    <score-part id="P1">
      <part-name>Drums</part-name>
      <score-instrument id="P1-X4">
        <instrument-name>Snare Drum</instrument-name>
      </score-instrument>
      <score-instrument id="P1-X2">
        <instrument-name>Kick Drum</instrument-name>
      </score-instrument>
      <score-instrument id="P1-X13">
        <instrument-name>Crash Cymbal</instrument-name>
      </score-instrument>
      <score-instrument id="P1-X6">
        <instrument-name>Hi-Hat%g Closed</instrument-name>
      </score-instrument>
      <midi-instrument id="P1-X4">
        <midi-channel>10</midi-channel>
        <midi-program>1</midi-program>
        <midi-unpitched>39</midi-unpitched>
      </midi-instrument>
      <midi-instrument id="P1-X2">
        <midi-channel>10</midi-channel>
        <midi-program>1</midi-program>
        <midi-unpitched>37</midi-unpitched>
      </midi-instrument>
      <midi-instrument id="P1-X13">
        <midi-channel>10</midi-channel>
        <midi-program>1</midi-program>
        <midi-unpitched>50</midi-unpitched>
      </midi-instrument>
      <midi-instrument id="P1-X6">
        <midi-channel>10</midi-channel>
        <midi-program>1</midi-program>
        <midi-unpitched>43</midi-unpitched>
      </midi-instrument>
    </score-part>
    <score-part id="P2">
      <part-name>Cowbell</part-name>
      <score-instrument id="P2-X1">
        <instrument-name>Cowbell</instrument-name>
      </score-instrument>
      <midi-instrument id="P2-X1">
        <midi-channel>10</midi-channel>
        <midi-program>1</midi-program>
        <midi-unpitched>57</midi-unpitched>
      </midi-instrument>
    </score-part>
  </part-list>
```

## Notehead shapes

- `<notehead>` specifies alternate notehead shapes.
- MusicXML playback can distinguish instruments using different `<instrument>` elements.
- Different notehead shapes distinguish different instruments on the same staff line.
- The `filled` attribute indicates a filled or hollow shape for enclosed shapes such as `normal`, `diamond`, `triangle`, and `square`.
- The `filled` attribute is also useful for multi-part piano music, including a downstem half note sharing a hollow notehead with an upstem eighth note.
- An eighth note can specify an unfilled normal notehead to display correctly when moving between notation programs.

### `<notehead>` values

- `slash`
- `triangle`
- `diamond`
- `square`
- `cross`
- `x`
- `circle-x`
- `normal`
- `cluster`
- `inverted triangle`
- `arrow down`
- `arrow up`
- `slashed`
- `back slashed`
- `do`
- `re`
- `mi`
- `fa`
- `so`
- `la`
- `ti`

The first two notes of the cymbal/hi-hat line:

```xml
      <note default-x="78">
        <unpitched>
          <display-step>B</display-step>
          <display-octave>3</display-octave>
        </unpitched>
        <duration>1</duration>
        <instrument id="P1-X13"/>
        <voice>1</voice>
        <type>eighth</type>
        <stem default-y="40">up</stem>
        <notehead filled="no">diamond</notehead>
        <beam number="1">begin</beam>
      </note>
      <note default-x="109">
        <unpitched>
          <display-step>B</display-step>
          <display-octave>3</display-octave>
        </unpitched>
        <duration>1</duration>
        <instrument id="P1-X6"/>
        <voice>1</voice>
        <type>eighth</type>
        <stem default-y="40">up</stem>
        <notehead>x</notehead>
        <beam number="1">continue</beam>
      </note>
```

## Measure styles and repeats

- One-bar repeat symbols, similar repeats, and multimeasure rests are represented using `<measure-style>`.
- The second bar of the cowbell part is specified as the first bar: four notes with `<display-step>E</display-step>`, `<display-octave>4</display-octave>`, and instrument `P2-X1`.
- The beginning of the one-measure repeat style is indicated with `<measure-repeat type="start">1</measure-repeat>`.

```xml
    <measure number="2">
      <attributes>
        <measure-style>
          <measure-repeat type="start">1</measure-repeat>
        </measure-style>
      </attributes>
```

## Stated design goals and limitations

- Percussion instruments can be either pitched or unpitched.
- Instruments with definite pitch, such as timpani or mallet instruments, are handled using normal musical notation.
- For instruments without definite pitch, vertical space represents different instruments rather than pitch.
- More percussion instruments may be handled by one player than can fit into the lines on a staff.
- A single unpitched instrument may be notated on a staff with fewer lines, avoiding wasted vertical space on a 5-line staff.
- MusicXML allows percussion music to be represented both as heard and as notated.
- Using `<pitch>` for notes without definite pitch would be misleading.
- An analysis program looking for repeated B notes should not return this piece of music.
- An analysis program looking for repeated F-sharps based on the General MIDI pitch for a closed hi-hat should not return this piece of music.
- The page does not provide syntax or named features for chords/harmony.
- The page does not provide syntax or named features for bend, vibrato, pressure, timbre, continuous controllers (CC), micro-timing, or articulation.

## Verbatim element syntax and structure

- Parent element: `<technical>`
- `<bend>`
- `<bend-alter>` (Required)
- Zero or one of:
  - `<pre-bend>`
  - `<release>`
- `<with-bar>` (Optional)

## Named bend features

- The `<bend>` element is used in guitar notation and tablature.
- A single note with a bend and release will contain two `<bend>` elements:
  - The first represents the bend.
  - The second represents the release.
- `accelerate`: Does the bend accelerate during playback? Default is `"no"`.
- `beats`: The number of discrete elements, like MIDI pitch bends, used to represent a continuous bend or slide. Default is `4`.
- `first-beat`: The percentage of the duration for starting a bend. Default is `25`.
- `last-beat`: The percentage of the duration for ending a bend. Default is `75`.
- `shape`: Distinguishes between:
  - The angled bend symbols commonly used in standard notation.
  - The curved bend symbols commonly used in both tablature and standard notation.
- `with-bar`: Optional child element.

## Attributes

| Name | Type | Required? | Description |
|---|---|---:|---|
| `accelerate` | `yes-no` | No | Does the bend accelerate during playback? Default is `"no"`. |
| `beats` | `trill-beats` | No | The number of discrete elements (like MIDI pitch bends) used to represent a continuous bend or slide. Default is 4. |
| `color` | `color` | No | Indicates the color of an element. |
| `default-x` | `tenths` | No | Changes the computation of the default horizontal position. The origin is changed relative to the left-hand side of the note or the musical position within the bar. Positive x is right and negative x is left. This attribute provides higher-resolution positioning data than the `<offset>` element. Applications reading a MusicXML file that can understand both features should generally rely on this attribute for its greater accuracy. |
| `default-y` | `tenths` | No | Changes the computation of the default vertical position. The origin is changed relative to the top line of the staff. Positive y is up and negative y is down. ## Harmony and chord features

- The `<harmony>` element represents:
  - Harmony analysis.
  - Chord symbols in popular music.
  - Functional harmony analysis in classical music.
- Each individual chord includes a required `<kind>` element and is called a “harmony-chord.”
- Stacked chords or secondary functions are represented using a sequence of harmony-chords.
- A `<root>` element is generally used with pop chord symbols.
- A `<numeral>` element is generally used with classical functional harmony and Nashville numbers.
- `<root>` and `<numeral>` are an either/or choice to avoid data inconsistency.
- The `<function>` element represents Roman numerals with Roman numeral text.
- The `<function>` element has been deprecated as of MusicXML 4.0.
- The `print-object` attribute controls whether anything is printed due to the `<harmony>` element.
- The print suggestion attributes set defaults for the harmony, but individual elements can override these values.

## Content model

In this order:

1. One or more harmony-chords, each containing:
   - Exactly one of:
     - `<root>`
     - `<numeral>`
     - `<function>`
   - `<kind>` — required
   - `<inversion>` — optional
   - `<bass>` — optional
   - `<degree>` — zero or more times
2. `<frame>` — optional
3. `<offset>` — optional
4. In this order:
   - `<footnote>` — optional
   - `<level>` — optional
5. `<staff>` — optional
